props.title: Man Bites Dog

sections.content: Man Bites Dog revolutionized mockumentary horror with its pitch-black satire of media violence. Shot in grainy black-and-white, this Belgian film follows a documentary crew recording serial killer Ben as he philosophizes between murders. It predated and influenced later found-footage horror like The Blair Witch Project (1999) and Behind the Mask: The Rise of Leslie Vernon (2006). The film's genius lies in making viewers complicit - we laugh at Ben's charismatic monologues, then recoil at brutal violence, forcing us to confront our own voyeuristic entertainment.

sections.content: The film sparked a wave of controversial mockumentaries examining violence and media complicity. Series 7: The Contenders (2001) imagined a reality show where contestants must kill each other, while The Last Horror Movie (2003) featured a serial killer forcing his videographer to document his crimes. These films challenge audience bloodlust by removing the safety buffer of traditional narrative distance. SUBHEAD: Media Complicity and Found Footage Evolution

The documentary crew's gradual corruption from observers to participants marked a crucial evolution in found footage horror. While Cannibal Holocaust (1980) previously explored similar themes, Man Bites Dog's intimate portrait format created a more insidious commentary on media ethics. This influence echoes through films like Lake Mungo (2008) and The Bay (2012), where documentary formats lend credibility to horror.
